source_text: Quia videlicet et simplicius quaepiam dixerint, et quodcumque aliud speculantes, non habuerint necessitatem a latere surgentibus quaestionibus obviandi. Cum enim crebro laudaverint coniugia, et nullam in corporibus affectionem a diabolo insertam putarint, nec regno diaboli divina opera, id est naturae membra, subiecerint, sed et a Deo instituta coniugia ac benedictione donata, liberumque arbitrium, prout opportunitas attulit, explicarint; humanum est ut non stare in societate vestri sceleris iudicentur, si in scripturis illorum aut ambigue, aut negligenter quaepiam locata deprehenditis. Quomodo enim non praeiudicat Scripturis sanctis, quod omnes haereses aliquibus se earum testimoniis occulunt ac nituntur tueri; ita etiam catholicorum virorum famam propter quaepiam incautius fusa, non patiemur addici. Neque enim habuerunt intentionem illi, aut damnandi nuptias, aut liberum arbitrium denegandi, vel innocentiam sauciandi; quam si habuissent, non vestrum dogma firmassent, sed honorem officii perdidissent.
pass_a_gloss: Because namely they both said some things more simply, and, speculating some other thing, did not have a necessity of meeting questions rising from the side. For when they frequently praised marriages, and thought no affection in bodies inserted by the devil, nor subjected divine works, that is members of nature, to the devil's kingdom, but explained both marriages instituted by God and given by blessing, and free decision, as opportunity brought; it is human that they not be judged to stand in the society of your crime, if in their writings you catch some things placed either ambiguously or negligently. For as what all heresies hide themselves by some testimonies of them and strive to protect does not prejudge the holy Scriptures; so also we will not suffer the fame of catholic men to be assigned on account of some things poured more incautiously. For they did not have an intention either of condemning marriages, or of denying free decision, or of wounding innocence; which if they had had, they would not have firmed your dogma, but would have lost the honor of office.

lemmas.lexica: LS necessitas; Blaise vs free choice
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS liber=free; Blaise unde liberum est abstinere
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS nuptiae; Blaise Christian marriage as God's work

pass_b_english: They may have spoken somewhat simply, or, while examining some other subject, may have had no need to meet questions arising on the side. They frequently praised marriage, thought no bodily feeling had been implanted by the devil, and did not subject God’s works—the members of nature—to the devil’s kingdom. They also explained, as occasions arose, marriage instituted by God and granted his blessing, and free choice. It is therefore humane to judge that they do not stand in fellowship with your wickedness if you find certain things ambiguously or carelessly placed in their writings. Just as the fact that all heresies conceal themselves behind some testimonies of holy Scripture and try to defend themselves by them does not count against Scripture, so I will not allow the reputation of catholic men to be surrendered because of some words poured out less cautiously. They did not intend to condemn marriage, deny free choice, or wound innocence. If they had intended this, they would not have strengthened your doctrine; they would have lost the honor of their office.

choices.why: Julian defends marriage as God's work against the charge that generation transmits sin.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
